notes.meaning: The craftsmen used blue, purple, and scarlet yarns to make the holy garments for Aaron and his sons. These special clothes were set apart only for ministering in the sanctuary, not for everyday wear or personal pride. The workers followed every detail just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

Bezalel made the sacred ephod, an ornate sleeveless vest worn by the high priest. It was woven from fine linen, brightly colored yarns, and pure gold thread. This beautiful vest showed the dignity and sacred duty of the priestly office.

The metalworkers hammered pure gold into paper-thin sheets and cut them into thin wires. They then carefully wove these gold threads into the colored wool and linen. This skillful work gave the holy garment a rich, lasting brilliance fit for worship before God.

The workers made two shoulder straps for the ephod and attached them to its top corners. These straps connected the front and back pieces of the vest. They allowed the high priest to wear the heavy garment securely as he served.

The waistband was woven right into the ephod as one single piece rather than a separate belt. It used the exact same gold, linen, and colored yarns as the rest of the garment. This showed that the priest's service was undivided and done in complete obedience to God.

Two onyx stones were carved with the names of the twelve sons of Israel, six on each stone. The craftsmen mounted them in gold settings and fastened them onto the shoulder straps of the ephod. In this way, Aaron carried the memory and weight of the whole nation before the Lord.

The craftsmen made the breastpiece using the same skilled needlework as the ephod. It was woven from fine linen, gold threads, and blue, purple, and scarlet yarns. This sacred piece was worn over the chest of the high priest during worship.

The breastpiece was square, measuring about nine inches on each side. The workers folded it double to form a sturdy pocket or pouch. This pouch held the sacred lots used to seek God's direction for the people.

The workers placed four rows of precious gems on the breastpiece, with three stones in each row. The first row contained a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald; the second held a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond; and the third held a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst. Each jewel brought its own distinct beauty to the sacred garment.

The fourth row held a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper, each set into gold filigree. Every stone was carved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. This showed that each tribe was individually known and held dear by God.

The craftsmen braided chains of pure gold like cords to secure the breastpiece. They also made two gold settings and two gold rings, attaching the rings to the upper corners of the breastpiece. These pieces prepared the chest piece to be hung safely from the shoulders.

The workers fastened the two braided gold chains to the rings on the top corners of the breastpiece. Then they attached the other ends of the chains to the gold settings on the front shoulder straps of the ephod. This kept the breastpiece suspended firmly from above.

They made two more gold rings and placed them on the lower inside corners of the breastpiece. They also attached two matching gold rings to the bottom front of the ephod straps, right above the waistband. These lower rings were positioned to line up with each other.

The craftsmen tied the lower rings of the breastpiece to the rings on the ephod with a blue cord. This held the breastpiece firmly in place above the waistband so it would not flap loose while the high priest walked. Everything was done in exact obedience to the Lord's command to Moses.

The artisans made the robe worn beneath the ephod, weaving it entirely out of solid blue cloth. It was woven all in one piece rather than sewn together from scraps. This bright blue robe created a clean, rich backdrop for the colorful vest and breastpiece worn on top of it.
